Jovan Gerbscheid said:

Yes I am worried about implicit_reducible types having the lean#9077 problem. How are you planning to fix this?

My understanding was that lean#9077 is caused by the fact that instances are being unified implicitly. And obviously, an implicit_reducible type does not stop this implicit unification.

I thought it might make sense to start a new thread for this.

The underlying problem is a combination of two issues:

  • During instance search, if we obtain a value for an instance-implicit argument by unification of the expected and actual type of the instance, we don't synthesize it at all and just trust that the unified instance is good. This mostly happens because it is more efficient.
  • Sometimes, unfolding an instance can change its type w.r.t instance transparency, potentially leading to the assignment of an instance of the wrong type.

Mathlib-free MWE:

class P (α : Type) where p : Nat
class Q (α : Type) extends P α where
structure H (α : Type) {p : P α} [p' : P α] (h : p = p') where
class N (β : Type) where
instance inst (α : Type) [q : Q α] : N (H α (p := q.toP) rfl) where

@[implicit_reducible]
def Copy (α : Type) := α

@[implicit_reducible] instance pCopy [P E] : P (Copy E) := (inferInstance : P E)

/-
This should not work, but it does work:
`inst : N (H (Copy E) rfl)` needs `Q (Copy E)`, but we only have `iQ : Q E`, and these types are not instance-reducibly equal.

However, after instance resolution (`synthPending`) fails to synthesize `?q : Q (Copy E)`,
we syntesize it by unification:
`pCopy (inst := iQ.toP) =?= ?q.toP` (unfolding `pCopy` because it's implicit-reducible and we bumped transparency for `H`'s implicit argument `p`.)
`iQ.toP =?= ?q.toP`
`iQ =?= ?q` (types match at implicit transparency)

So we assign `(?q : Q (Copy E)) := (iQ : Q E)`.
-/

variable (E : Type) [iQ : Q E] in
#synth N (H (Copy E) rfl)

The fix I am working on solves this by being more careful during unification. When we assign an instance to an instance-implicit argument mvar during instance search, we check its type at instance transparency (with some internal technical subtleties that I mostly figured out).

  1. If the assigned instance is of the correct type, all good; just use the instance assigned by unification.
  2. If it is of the wrong type, synthesize the instance instead, then verify that the synthesized instance matches the unified one.

I extensively tested this over the last few weeks (and it was also the reason for the DM I sent you some days ago). It fixes #9077 and there are ~40 breaking sites in all of Mathlib, which I am working my way through right now.

Sorry, that # Fix is a leftover from an earlier stage where I provided example's with the proposed fixes that I removed since then (too verbose for merging; if you are interested, I can provide a branch with them restored).

Regarding how to interpret the suggested fixes: One should first find a way to remove the respectTransparency false annotation if present. After that, most of the instanceTypes false annotations become obsolete, too. I manually studied the traces and verified that every single suggested fix works, so that shouldn't be the crux, but I ultimately didn't want to make more decisions than necessary in an adaptation branch, only suggesting ones that seemed right to me. My Mathlib expertise is limited.

My hope is that the adaptation notes explain what goes wrong: in many cases, some instance that is needed fails to be synthesized, or it can be synthesized, but Lean fails to see that the synthesized instance is definitionally equal (at implicit transparency) to the one that is expected. In such a case, one can either make more definitions implicit-reducible, or one can decide that the proof does "defeq abuse" and restructure it. This is not a decision I can make for mathlib; implicit_reducible is a feature that allows you to control how much reduction you want Lean to do, potentially at a performance cost. So it is a trade-off, although there are some rules of thumb (see below).

I'm still unsure what explanation helps people most when thinking about implicit reducibility in practice. How about this?

Consider a definition def x : C := sorry. Here are some rules of thumb that can be violated with good reason:

  • Is C a class type? Then x should be instance-reducible.
  • Is C a non-class type? Then x should be reducible (if it's an abbreviation), implicit-reducible (if you want it to be opaque for instance search, e.g. for type aliases) or irreducible. Consider using a one-field structure if possible.
  • Is x intended to be used in types? Then it should be reducible, implicit-reducible or irreducible, too.
  • Is x a functor? Then x should be implicit-reducible, because x.obj frequently appears in types and Lean needs to be able to unfold it when checking whether two types are the same, at implicit transparency.
  • Does x need to be unfolded in order to prevent instance diamonds? Then it should be at least implicit-reducible. (I intentionally wrote implicit here, not instance)
  • Is x expensive to unfold? Then avoid making it implicit-reducible. If this rule contradicts the others, then you should consider restructuring the library to reduce the unfolding that is needed.

Is this a genre of explanation that would be useful to codify somewhere?

Regarding the two cases you mentioned, I'd reason about them as follows.

  • TangentSpace is currently a semireducible type alias. It should become either a one-field structure, irreducible or implicit-reducible per the rules of thumb. Making it implicit-reducible is the easiest fix without restructuring the library, although I heard that there are intentions to reduce the level of unfolding necessary for it. I tried out making it implicit-reducible and it did not deteriorate Mathlib's benchmark performance.
  • LinearMap.ker feels more like a Mathlib-specific judgment call. Do you want this to be unfolded when Lean compares types, implicit arguments or resolves instance diamonds? Do you fear excessive unfolding of its carrier set?

Reading between the lines, are things going in a direction where "never use semreducible" becomes a rule?

Isn't TangentSpace the reason why this whole thing was started? If it becomes implicit-reducible, then we are back at the problems that Sebastien had? Namely, E has a norm, but then you want to define a different norm on TangentSpace that is not equal to the original one. So if TangentSpace was implicit-reducible, the typeclass search might find the wrong instance (your second to last point, right?)
Implicit-reducible definitions are not unfolded during instance search. Only instance-reducible and reducible definitions are.
The discussion from #mathlib4 > 4.33.0-rc1 Multiple `respectTransparency`-related issues @ 💬 is also relevant for whether it is possible to make TangentSpace implicit-reducible.

Eric Wieser said:

Reading between the lines, are things going in a direction where "never use semreducible" becomes a rule?

Only for type definitions; these should almost never be semireducible. Apart from that, definitely not. Many definitions shouldn't be unfolded automatically by automation like simp, grind etc.; otherwise nothing would have been won except renaming semireducible to implicit_reducible.

Consider the list as "if one of these cases matches, consider making it implicit-reducible; otherwise semireducible (or sometimes something else) is usually a good choice".

Julia Markus Himmel said:

Implicit-reducible definitions are not unfolded during instance search. Only instance-reducible and reducible definitions are.

To clarify, this will be true after I merge my fix that is discussed in this thread; currently, the lean4#9077 bug violates this.
